reasoning: Form VI past with an initial cluster; ق is a glottal stop in this everyday verb. Covers both a shouting match and a physical fight.
News and political vocabulary, where ق keeps [q]. The word-initial hamza is on a vowel seat; the shadda doubles the l.
Long oo. In Ramallah zooj is mostly heard for husband, and a pair of shoes or socks is jooz, as in jooz sharaab.
Long ii in the first syllable, then two short a vowels. Used for both the building and the art form.
Both ق are glottal stops; ط is emphatic T. The first noun is in construct, so its taa marbuta is pronounced -et and written ت for the voice.
Taa marbuta after ج is e; plural nataa'ij. Used for exam results as well as consequences.
Shadda doubles the b; plural shabaabiik. The ordinary Palestinian word for a window, over MSA naafidhe.
Dialectal mit- participle rather than MSA mutafaaji'; the final hamza is written '. Feminine mitfaaj'a.

The hamza after the bi- prefix is written. Urban Palestinian has no interdental [dh] outside recitation, so ذ comes out z and the Arabic is respelt accordingly; more formal than plain in shaa' allah, as the English says.

In the 'modern' sense ث comes out s in urban Palestinian, so the Arabic is respelt حَدِيس; careful or religious speech keeps 7adiith, which is also the noun for a Prophetic tradition. Everyday speech often just uses jdiid.

reasoning: waajhe is the front or facade of a building, and figuratively a front for something. The glass display window of a shop is fitriine in Ramallah.
ط is emphatic T. Heard in educated speech but carries a written flavour; the conversational Ramallah equivalent is ma daam.
The hamza of MSA ra's is lost and the vowel lengthens, raas; plural ruus. Also used for the top of something.
3eeb has a long ee; ش is a sun letter, giving ish-shoom. A set exclamation of reproach at behaviour that is beneath someone.
ث surfaces as s in this common word, so the Arabic is respelt مُمَسِّل; the shadda doubles the s. The same word also means a representative.
Shadda doubles the t; long uu in the second syllable. The Levantine salad with toasted bread and sumac.
Negative imperative with la plus the bare imperfect, no b- prefix. Masculine addressee, so no -i ending.
shu is the Palestinian what; ب is a moon letter so the article stays il-. The English word is borrowed whole, with the Arabic kalmet is-sirr used only in formal writing.
The final hamza of shaa' is written, as in maa shaa'. Said constantly in Ramallah, both sincerely and as a soft maybe.
ka'anni contracts to kaanni in speech, which is what the headword spelling shows; the shadda doubles the n. Said when one's words have had no effect.
ص is emphatic S and ق is a glottal stop; taa marbuta after ق is a. Voluntary almsgiving, as against the obligatory zakaa.
Urban Palestinian says ذ as z here, il-azaan, so the Arabic is respelt with ز for the voice. The word-initial hamza is on a vowel seat.
Three short vowels, stress on the first syllable. The adjective is faransi.
Literally rancid, of oil or butter, and used of people and situations that are tiresome or cringeworthy. Feminine zankha.
